stages.name: National income
stages.title: Marginal propensities
stages.sub: How extra national income splits between saving, tax and imports, and what that means for withdrawals.

steps.q: The whole country's income rises by £100 this year. Does every extra pound get spent on domestic goods, or does some of it go elsewhere?
steps.wrong: All of it gets spent on domestic goods
steps.hint: Think about your own pay rise: does all of it go straight into shops?

steps.q: Of that extra £100 of national income, £20 ends up sitting unspent in bank accounts. What fraction of the extra income was that?
steps.right: 0.2, the share saved rather than spent
steps.hint: A propensity is a share of the extra income, not the raw pound amount.

steps.q: Saving, tax and imports are the three ways extra income can leak out of domestic spending. Out of the £100, £20 was saved, £30 taxed and £10 spent on imports. What fraction of the £100 left domestic spending in total?
steps.right: 0.6, the combined share that leaked out
steps.hint: Add the three fractions together rather than picking just one.
